ai-at-work.title: Cisco Partner Summit: Five insights that will define the channel in the AI era
ai-at-work.excerpt: For most of its 30-year history, Cisco Partner Summit has focused on how partners sell Cisco Systems Inc. technology. This year’s event in Vancouver was about something different: how partners make mo
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Cisco's partner summit shifted focus from selling boxes to helping partners build sustainable AI-driven business models in a world where individual transactions matter less. This matters because it signals that the entire vendor ecosystem is finally accepting that AI commoditizes products faster than partners can inventory them, forcing a pivot toward services and outcomes. The real takeaway is that after 30 years of "sell more stuff," the channel is learning what consultants figured out in 2015: the margin is in the advice, not the appliance.

tools-tech.title: Github competitor Entire is live now – how the agent-first platform works
tools-tech.excerpt: Now that agents are writing so much code, Entire is trying to reinvent the coding platform itself.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Entire has launched as a GitHub alternative built specifically around AI agents doing the actual coding work rather than humans. This matters because digital workplace teams are suddenly managing a hybrid workforce where code gets written by both people and AI, which means your collaboration platforms need to handle that reality or become obsolete fast. Honestly, watching startups chase every AI trend gets old, but if Entire actually solves the "how do we version control and review code written by agents" problem, they've found something worth building instead of just slapping AI onto existing tools.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft Teams to get AI protection against phishing and fraud
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft is adding a new AI-powered security feature to Teams aimed at detecting phishing, scams, and identity theft by analyzing conversations, Bleeping Computer reports. Instead of primarily checki
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft is rolling out an AI feature for Teams that analyzes message content itself to catch phishing and fraud attempts, rather than just flagging dodgy links and files. This matters because most phishing attacks succeed through social engineering, not malware, so catching suspicious behavior in actual conversations could save your organization from real financial and data losses. Finally, someone decided the answer to "how do we stop people from getting scammed" isn't just "block the bad URL" but "maybe read what people are actually saying to each other." About time.

tools-tech.title: Technology has changed. So should the conversation.
tools-tech.excerpt: I’ve spent more than 20 years talking about technology and how it can improve people’s lives. For most of that time, I was optimistic about the future. I still believe tech can make our lives better.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Computerworld's veteran tech commentator is calling out the industry for abandoning the basic question of whether technology actually improves people's lives, arguing we need more critical examination instead of blind optimism. For digital workplace professionals, this lands hard because we're the ones dealing with the tools nobody actually asked for that somehow ended up slowing down productivity instead of speeding it up. After three decades watching companies bolt on features nobody needs, I'm with this one: the next time a vendor promises transformation, ask them to prove it doesn't make your job worse first.

digital-culture.title: Entrepreneurship might be the key to a longer life
digital-culture.excerpt: If you thought entrepreneurship was too stressful a path to venture down, you might want to reassess. A new study found that there may be a surprising benefit to starting a business: longevity. The st
digital-culture.dwp_take: Researchers at Stevens Institute of Technology found that entrepreneurs actually live longer than their non-business-owning peers, contradicting the assumption that startup stress kills you faster. This matters to digital workplace folks because remote work and independent projects are blurring the line between employment and entrepreneurship, meaning more of us might be accidentally extending our lifespans through side hustles. Of course, the real question is whether entrepreneurs live longer or just feel like they're living longer because they're checking Slack at 2am on a Sunday.

digital-culture.title: Kevin O’Leary has one rule for giving money to family. It works at any income
digital-culture.excerpt: It’s pretty hard to feel bad for billionaires, but according to a host of incredibly wealthy people there’s one aspect of being filthy rich that is no fun at all: deciding what to do when friends and
digital-culture.dwp_take: Kevin O'Leary shared his personal rule for handling money requests from family: apparently he treats it like a business decision rather than an emotional one. This matters to workplace culture because how leaders handle money and boundaries at home often mirrors how they handle resources and people decisions at work, which means understanding their personal philosophy can actually tell you something about their management style. My take: if you need a billionaire's advice on saying no to family, maybe the real problem isn't the rule but that you haven't figured out your own values yet.

digital-culture.title: Why Anthropic’s IPO Prospectus Is Missing So Many Key Figures
digital-culture.excerpt: Anthropic’s S-1 filing is hundreds of pages long—and it leaves out quite a few financial details. “Anthropic owes investors more information,” one analyst tells WIRED.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Anthropic's IPO filing is loaded with pages but somehow manages to hide the actual financial numbers that matter, which is either a bold strategy or a masterclass in "look busy." For those of us building digital workplaces around AI tools, this opacity matters because we need to understand whether these vendors are actually sustainable or just expensive experiments with great marketing. The old saying goes that if you can't understand how a company makes money, you probably shouldn't bet your enterprise stack on their staying power for the next five years.

digital-culture.title: The Anthropic S-1 Filing Is Also an AI Doomsday Primer
digital-culture.excerpt: Anthropic thinks “closing the loop” is the best path to AI triumph—and a recipe for “existential” threats to humanity.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Anthropic's IPO filing basically admits that the more they optimize their AI systems, the closer they get to creating something that could pose existential risks to humanity. For digital workplace folks, this matters because we're about to deploy AI tools into our organizations without fully understanding the long-term safety implications of what we're building. Here's the thing: if the people actually making the AI are worried about doomsday scenarios in their official regulatory filings, maybe we should all pump the brakes on the "AI solves everything" narrative and actually think through what we're inviting into our offices.
